findings.title: Insight tab is reachable by Cmd+S / save / refresh paths that operate on tab.url without checking tab.kind — writes a hidden file `.insight-<uuid>` into the user's folder
findings.description:
`startRecursiveInsight()` (WorkspaceManager.swift:1399) constructs a placeholder URL `folderURL.appendingPathComponent(".insight-<uuid>")` and appends an `OpenTab` with that URL via `tabsStore.appendTab(tab, activate: true)`. This makes the insight tab the active tab. Three independent code paths read `openTabs[activeTabIndex].url` and perform real filesystem I/O on it without inspecting `tab.kind`:
  1. `saveActiveFile()` (WorkspaceManager.swift:1149) → `saveFile(at:)` (L1533-1546) → `try tab.content.write(to: tab.url, ...)` — bound to Cmd+S via `MarkViewApp.swift:189-194` and to the JS bridge `bridgeSaveRequested` (EditorView.swift:534).
  2. `reloadActiveTabFromDisk()` (WorkspaceManager.swift:1664) → `try? String(contentsOf: tab.url, ...)` — bound to the JS refresh button via `bridgeRefreshRequested` (EditorView.swift:580).
  3. `updateActiveTabContent` (L1635) sets `tab.isModified = true` if JS posts a `documentEdited` event while an insight tab is active — this primes case 1 by marking the insight tab dirty.

Reproduction: open a folder, start Recursive Insight, hit Cmd+S while the insight tab is active. Result: `<folderURL>/.insight-<uuid>` is created on disk containing whatever happens to be in `tab.content` (currently `""`, but will become non-empty if any code path ever sets `tab.content` for an insight tab — translateDocument-style flows, or future feature). Worse, on `bridgeRefreshRequested`, if the user previously hit Cmd+S, the now-existing hidden file is read back and clobbers `tab.content`. Worse still — the spec (lines 36-39) explicitly says "This URL is never written to disk", which the codebase silently violates because the design assumes file-tab semantics for every active tab.

Decision 10 §7 + the rationale at tech-spec L238 explicitly call out NSSavePanel/file-write paths as a security boundary; this leak bypasses NSSavePanel entirely and writes to a user-specified folder using a path that includes a server-generated UUID without the user ever seeing a prompt. While the immediate impact is small (zero-byte hidden file in the user's folder), it is a real silent filesystem write that violates the spec's invariant and is the seed of bigger problems if downstream features grow `tab.content` for insight tabs.
findings.location: MarkView/Models/WorkspaceManager.swift:1149 (saveActiveFile), :1533-1546 (saveFile), :1664-1678 (reloadActiveTabFromDisk), :1399-1408 (placeholder URL creation + appendTab), MarkView/App/MarkViewApp.swift:189-194 (Cmd+S binding), MarkView/Views/EditorView.swift:534-538 (bridgeSaveRequested), :580-590 (bridgeRefreshRequested)
findings.impact: Silent unintended filesystem write into a user-trusted folder (creates `<folderURL>/.insight-<uuid>`). Violates the explicit tech-spec invariant that the placeholder URL is never written to disk. Today: empty file with a UUID in its name appears in the user's folder. Tomorrow: any code path that grows insight tab `content` (highly plausible — bridge edit events, autosave, content sync) leaks streaming summary text, including untrusted LLM output, to disk without user consent and without going through the sanitized `saveInsightNode` pipeline. Also opens a state-corruption channel: `bridgeRefreshRequested` would read the hidden file back into `tab.content`, breaking `currentMarkdown(for:)` invariants.
findings.cwe: CWE-73 (External Control of File Name or Path), CWE-732 (Incorrect Permission Assignment for Critical Resource)

findings.title: Filename sanitization keeps the empty-stem case but does not defend against `.` / `..` produced after collapse — `node.title == "..."` yields default filename `"insight"` only by accident
findings.description:
`sanitizeInsightFilename` (WorkspaceManager.swift:1518-1530) maps every non-alphanumeric/underscore character to `_`, then collapses runs of `_` via `split(separator:"_", omittingEmptySubsequences: true).joined(separator:"_")`. The collapse step handles the empty case correctly, but the function does NOT explicitly trim or reject results that NSSavePanel would interpret as path components (`.`, `..`). For a node title like `"."` or `".."`, every character is non-alphanumeric → mapped to `_` → collapse → `"_"` (one underscore) → not empty → returned. So far so good: NSSavePanel sees `_` as nameField. But the spec (Decision 10 §7 / line 61 of tasks/7.md) says: "trim leading/trailing `_`". The current implementation does NOT trim — it relies on `omittingEmptySubsequences: true` to collapse runs but a single leading or trailing `_` survives (e.g., title `"_foo"` → mapped `"_foo"` → split → `["foo"]` → joined `"foo"` — actually correct here since the leading `_` produces an empty leading subsequence which is omitted). Re-checking: `"_foo_".split(separator: "_", omittingEmptySubsequences: true)` → `["foo"]` → joined `"foo"`. So leading/trailing trim IS implicit. Spec is satisfied.

However, the function returns the unicode-letter set as-is for `Character.isLetter` — this includes characters like RTL override (U+202E), zero-width joiner (U+200D), and other invisible/control unicode that ARE classified as letters or are not mapped (`isLetter` is false for ZWJ but true for some RTL-categorized letters). Critically, NSSavePanel's `nameFieldStringValue` accepts unicode but the file ultimately written via `pickedURL.appendingPathExtension("md")` may be problematic on case-insensitive file systems or when synced via iCloud/Dropbox. More importantly, `Character.isNumber` accepts non-ASCII numeric characters (e.g., Arabic-Indic digits, Roman numerals — `Ⅻ` etc.) which the spec ([A-Za-z0-9_]) excludes by intent. The spec's `[A-Za-z0-9_]` is a strict ASCII-only set; the implementation is permissive.
findings.impact: Filenames may contain non-ASCII characters that the spec intentionally excludes. RTL-override characters in node titles can produce filenames that visually misrepresent their extension to a user inspecting Finder later (e.g., `safe[U+202E]dm.exe` displays as `safeexe.md`). For Recursive Insight saves this is a low-likelihood but real risk: the node title comes from LLM output (the model is asked to produce titles), and titles flow through this function unchanged for any unicode that is `isLetter` or `isNumber`. Defense-in-depth violation: the spec named ASCII-only for a reason.

findings.title: `UTType(filenameExtension: "md")!` force-unwrap will crash the app if the system's UT registry has no entry for `md`
findings.description: WorkspaceManager.swift:1490: `panel.allowedContentTypes = [.init(filenameExtension: "md")!]`. `UTType.init?(filenameExtension:)` is failable and returns `nil` when the OS cannot resolve the extension to a known type. While `md` is virtually always registered on macOS 11+, the force-unwrap turns a missing/conflicting Launch Services registration (e.g., a corrupt user profile, an unusual macOS minor version, or a future deprecation) into a hard crash on user-clicks-Save. There is no `import UniformTypeIdentifiers` at the top of the file — currently transitive via SwiftUI, which is brittle.
findings.impact: Denial of service on the Save action (process crash). User loses the insight session (and any other tab state). Crash is reachable purely from a user click — no attacker required. While the failure is unlikely in practice, the cost (zero) of a fallback path is far less than the cost of a single user-reported crash.
findings.recommendation:
Use a safe fallback or skip `allowedContentTypes` entirely (NSSavePanel works without it):
```swift
import UniformTypeIdentifiers   // make the dependency explicit
...
if let mdType = UTType(filenameExtension: "md") {
    panel.allowedContentTypes = [mdType]
}
panel.allowedFileTypes = ["md"]   // legacy fallback also works on every macOS
```
The `.md` extension is force-applied below at L1497-1502 already, so the panel's content-type filter is purely cosmetic — no security loss in dropping it on failure.
findings.cwe: CWE-754 (Improper Check for Unusual or Exceptional Conditions)

findings.title: NSLog of unsanitized `sessionId` / `nodeId` from JS bridge (no length cap, no character validation)
findings.description:
All five forwarders (WorkspaceManager.swift:1430, 1439, 1443, 1453, 1457, 1466, 1475) and `findInsightSession` callers pass the raw `sessionId: String` straight into `NSLog("...\(sessionId)...")`. The `sessionId` arrives from the JS bridge via `data?["sessionId"] as? String` (WebViewBridge.swift:193, 199, 204, 210, 215). Type-cast guarantees it's a String but does NOT validate it is a UUID, does NOT cap its length, and does NOT strip control characters. A compromised JS context (post-XSS via prompt injection per Decision 10 §238) can post arbitrary strings via `webkit.messageHandlers.markdownHandler.postMessage`, including:
  - newlines + `[Insight]`-prefixed fake log entries to spoof logs (log injection / forgery)
  - megabytes of payload to fill `os_log` / Console.app and the file system
  - terminal control sequences if logs are tail-followed in iTerm

For `nodeId`, the breadcrumb forwarder DOES validate via `UUID(uuidString:)` — good — but it logs the invalid value first (L1457: `NSLog("[Insight] didRequestInsightBreadcrumb: invalid nodeId \(nodeId)")`) which propagates the same issue.
findings.impact: Log injection: an attacker who lands an XSS in the insight WebView (the explicit threat model in Decision 10) can forge or fill operator-visible log entries. While not directly exploitable, it complicates incident response (a planted line like `[Insight] valid sessionId X — Cmd+S Save dispatched OK` could mask real malicious activity). Also a small denial-of-service vector via log size on `os_log` rate caps.

findings.title: `saveInsightNode` does not honor sandbox security-scoped resource semantics — outside-of-scope writes work only because the app sandbox is OFF
findings.description: The save handler (WorkspaceManager.swift:1488-1512) writes to `pickedURL` returned from NSSavePanel without calling `startAccessingSecurityScopedResource()` / `stopAccessingSecurityScopedResource()`. This is fine TODAY because the project's entitlements have the app sandbox disabled (per the `Sandbox off` reference in commit message `9787b35` and tech-spec L238: "Sandbox is OFF"). If the sandbox is ever re-enabled (a reasonable hardening step), every write outside the user-granted Powerbox scope will silently fail with `EPERM` and produce an `NSAlert` saying "could not save" — confusing for the user and a regression no one will trace.
findings.impact: Future-only: if sandbox is re-enabled, save fails for any path outside the app's granted scope. No present-day exploit. Listed as minor because the design choice (sandbox off) is documented and intentional.

findings.title: Coordinator forwarders wrap synchronous calls in `Task { @MainActor in ... }` — adds latency and decouples error context unnecessarily
findings.description:
EditorView.swift:598-626 wraps every insight forwarder in `Task { @MainActor in self.parent.workspaceManager.didRequestInsight…(...) }`. The wrapper is needed by the existing translate/save methods because `WebViewBridgeDelegate` methods are not `@MainActor`-isolated by the protocol declaration, and `WorkspaceManager` is `@MainActor`. However, this introduces:
  1. **Ordering hazard**: Two consecutive bridge messages (e.g., user clicks deep-dive then quickly clicks Up) become two unordered Tasks. Cooperative scheduling will usually preserve order on a single actor, but Swift makes no guarantee about Task enqueue order vs. submission order (per recent Swift evolution discussion). This is a latent ordering bug if the JS side ever bursts messages.
  2. **Lost call-site context**: any future addition that wants to know "did the bridge call succeed / fail / get rate-limited" cannot await the result through the Task wrapper. The current methods are all `Void`-returning so this is not yet an issue, but the pattern hides future error propagation.
  3. **Latency**: trampolining through Task means the Save NSSavePanel opens one runloop tick later than the click, which on heavy WebView loads can feel sluggish.

The spec (tasks/7.md L48-57) says "each method is a thin call to `parent.workspaceManager.<method>(sessionId:, ...)`" — the spec did not require Task wrapping.
findings.impact: Latent ordering hazard if bridge messages burst; minor latency on click→save; hidden error context. No present-day exploit.
findings.cwe: CWE-362 (Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization)

findings.title: `saveInsightNode` does not check whether the destination URL is inside the indexed folder being summarized — saving the summary BACK INTO the source folder will be picked up by the next Recursive Insight scan as input
findings.description:
If the user starts Recursive Insight on `~/notes/`, then clicks Save and picks `~/notes/Summary.md` as the destination, the saved summary file is now part of the folder. A subsequent `startRecursiveInsight()` on the same folder will scan and feed `Summary.md` (LLM-generated content) back into the model as a source `.md` — this is a feedback loop that pollutes the next root summary with the previous summary. While not a security issue per se (no path traversal, NSSavePanel saw the folder), it is a foot-gun the spec did not address.

Additionally: there is no check that the destination is writable BEFORE calling `panel.runModal()`, so the user picks a path then sees an error — minor UX, not a security issue.
findings.impact: LLM feedback-loop pollution on subsequent runs (model summarizes its own previous summary). Not exploitable, just data-quality regression.
findings.recommendation: Optional: warn the user (or refuse) if `finalURL` is inside the current `session.folderURL` — same containment check style as `scanMarkdownFiles` symlink defense. Or simpler: document the behavior in user-facing help and leave the behavior as-is. Consider non-blocking for this round.
